props.title: Seven Chances
props.initialSlug: Desperate bachelor races to marry by sundown

sections.content: Buster Keaton's Seven Chances stands as a masterclass in escalating physical comedy. The film's premise - a young man must marry by 7 PM to inherit $7 million - transforms from a simple romantic setup into one of silent cinema's most spectacular chase sequences. Keaton's trademark deadpan expression contrasts brilliantly with the increasing chaos around him, especially in the legendary finale where he outruns hundreds of would-be brides and an avalanche of boulders. The film influenced countless comedy-chase sequences, from It's a Mad, Mad, Mad, Mad World (1963) to The Blues Brothers (1980).

sections.content: The film's technical achievements remain impressive nearly 100 years later. Keaton performed his own stunts, including the dangerous boulder sequence shot on a steep hill in Bronson Canyon. The precision timing required for the bride chase - where hundreds of extras in wedding dresses pursue Keaton through Los Angeles streets - showcases his genius for large-scale comic choreography. This influenced later directors like Jackie Chan, who cited Seven Chances in developing his own action-comedy style for films like Project A (1983). SUBHEAD: Innovation in Silent Comedy

While contemporaries like Charlie Chaplin focused on pathos and character in films like The Kid (1921), Keaton pushed the boundaries of visual comedy through architectural precision and mechanical ingenuity. Seven Chances demonstrates his masterful understanding of escalating gags - starting with simple misunderstandings and building to city-wide chaos. This structure influenced generations of filmmakers, from the Marx Brothers' A Night at the Opera (1935) to modern action-comedies like Hot Fuzz (2007).
